h1: SEO for construction firms bidding on work worth crores
metaTitle: SEO for Construction Firms: Win Bigger Tenders
metaDescription: SEO for construction companies in India. We build capability, project and compliance pages that convince procurement before your first site meeting.
answer: For a construction firm, the search that matters happens after your name is already on a shortlist. Someone in procurement types your company name plus 'projects' or 'reviews' before the first meeting, and what they find decides whether you stay on it. Capability, completed-project and compliance pages are what they find — or don't.
takeaways: Your website's job is due diligence, not lead generation. Traffic is a poor proxy for whether it's working.
**Numbers or nothing.** A project page without built-up area, contract value band, duration and client type is a photo gallery with a caption.
Residential contracting and infrastructure contracting are two different businesses. Running both off one website confuses buyers and search engines equally.
`house construction cost per square feet in <city>` is where the search volume actually sits, and contractors have ceded it almost entirely to aggregators and lead portals.
Certifications and safety records belong in HTML, not in a 14 MB company-profile PDF nobody's crawler will open.

sections.h2: The search that decides the shortlist
body: Construction is not a category where a stranger reads a blog and fills a form for a ₹40-crore contract. The sequence runs the other way. You get recommended, or you respond to a tender, or a consultant puts three names in front of a client. Then somebody checks you.
That check is a search, and it is remarkably consistent. A procurement manager, a project consultant or a promoter's son-in-law types some combination of these before the first meeting:
bullets: `<firm name>` — do they even have a site, and does it look like a going concern
`<firm name> projects` or `<firm name> completed projects` — have they built anything like mine
`<firm name> reviews` — what does the internet say when you're not in the room
`<firm name> turnover` / `<firm name> ISO` — can they carry the scale, and are they certifiable
`<firm name> <city>` — are they real here, or a branch on a letterhead

callout.title: The PDF problem
callout.body: Most construction firms have all of this — in a company profile PDF built by a graphic designer, sitting behind a form or on a Drive link. Search engines index PDFs badly, the file takes forty seconds to open on a site office's connection, and nobody can link to page 7. Everything in that deck should exist as HTML pages. Keep the PDF as a download if you like; stop treating it as your website.

sections.h2: Two businesses, one website, and why that fails
body: The fastest way to make a construction website rank for nothing is to serve homeowners and procurement committees from the same pages. They search differently, they need different proof, and they convert on different things.

If you genuinely do both, separate them into distinct sections with distinct navigation, distinct landing pages and distinct enquiry routes. If one of them is under 15% of revenue, consider not competing for it at all.

body: Every construction firm claims capability. Almost none of them itemise it, which means the claim carries no weight and the page ranks for nothing. Itemised capability is simultaneously the most convincing page for a procurement reader and the most searchable, because procurement searches by equipment and by scope.
Publish the inventory. It's not confidential — your competitors have already seen your site anyway.
bullets: **Plant and equipment**, listed: batching plants and capacity, tower cranes, boom placers and concrete pumps, transit mixers, excavators, formwork systems by type, tipper and trailer fleet. Say what's owned versus hired — owned equipment is a genuine bidding advantage and nobody says so.
**Manpower strength** by category — engineers, supervisors, skilled and unskilled — and typical peak deployment on a single site.
**In-house versus subcontracted trades.** Civil, structural steel, MEP, finishes, façade. Procurement teams care intensely about this and ask it in every pre-bid meeting.

**Financial capacity**, at the level you're comfortable: annual turnover band, largest single contract executed, bank guarantee and bid-bond capacity. This decides whether you clear pre-qualification and it is a public fact in most tenders anyway.
**Geographic reach** — where you've mobilised, where you keep a permanent office, how far you'll travel for what contract size.

sections.h2: Project pages with numbers on them
body: A completed-project page is the highest-value content type in this industry and it takes forty minutes to write. Most firms publish a photograph and the client's name.
The data block is what does the work — for the reader, for the crawler, and for the AI systems increasingly summarising vendor shortlists.
numbered: **Scale in the unit that suits the work.** Built-up area in sq ft, road length in km, tankage in kilolitres, steel tonnage. Say which.
**Contract value**, as a band if the exact figure is contractual. "₹18–22 crore" is far more useful than "a prestigious project".

**Duration**, from mobilisation to handover, and whether you finished on programme. A firm that says "delivered in 19 months against a 17-month programme, delayed by a monsoon and a design revision" reads as more credible than one that claims it never slips.
**Client and consultants**, named, with permission. Named consultants are a referral channel: the consultant searches themselves and finds you.
**Scope**, precisely. Civil only, civil plus MEP, turnkey, design-build. Ambiguity here loses you bids you'd have won.
**Photographs with real alt text and captions**, plus a location. Site photos taken on a phone convert better than renders, because renders are what everyone shows.

callout.title: Live projects count too
callout.body: Ongoing sites are content most firms sit on until handover. A monthly progress update with a photo and a percentage-complete line is cheap to produce, proves the site actually exists, and gives you a publishing cadence without inventing blog topics. It also gives a prospect something to check the week they're deciding.

sections.h2: Certifications and safety are content, not a wall plaque
body: For institutional work, compliance is a qualification hurdle before it is a selling point. If your ISO certificates live as scanned JPEGs on an About page, nobody can verify them and no crawler can read them.

Give each a line of text with the standard, the certifying body, the scope covered and the validity period — ISO 9001 for quality, ISO 14001 for environmental management, ISO 45001 for occupational health and safety. Same for contractor registrations: CPWD or state PWD class, any NHAI or agency registration, GST and PAN, EPF and ESIC registration numbers, labour licences. Procurement teams check these; making them checkable is a trust signal in exactly the sense Google means by [E-E-A-T](/glossary/e-e-a-t).

Safety deserves its own page and almost nobody in Indian construction has one. Publish your EHS policy, safe man-hours accumulated, your lost-time injury frequency rate if you track it, your induction and toolbox-talk process, PPE standards, and how you handle height work. A promoter who has been burned by a site accident reads that page twice. Publish only what your records support — a safety claim you can't evidence is worse than no page.

sections.h2: Cost per square foot: the query you've ceded
body: `house construction cost per square feet in Bengaluru`, `2000 sq ft house construction cost`, `construction cost calculator India` — this is where the volume lives, and the results are dominated by aggregators, material brands and lead-selling portals. Contractors, who actually know the answer, are barely present.

It's winnable because you can be specific in ways an aggregator can't. A cost page needs package tiers — basic, standard, premium — with the actual specification behind each: which cement grade, which steel brand band, what flooring, what electrical and plumbing fittings, what's excluded. It needs a city, because Bengaluru and Patna are different numbers. And it needs a date, because steel and cement move enough within a year to make an undated page a liability.

Then link each tier to two completed homes that were built at it. That's the part no lead portal can copy, and it's why the page converts rather than merely ranking. If you take enquiries by phone — and in this industry you do — put the number and a WhatsApp link on the page, not behind a form.

sections.h2: Budget, timeline and what we guarantee
body: Our SEO starts at ₹75,000 a month, with smaller sites from ₹40,000, ex-GST. Construction firms with a residential arm usually need the higher tier, because there are two content programmes running at once. Full numbers are on [pricing](/pricing).

The honest timeline: brand and credential queries clean up fast — within weeks — because you're competing with your own absence, not with anyone else. Residential cost and `civil contractor near <area>` queries typically move inside three to six months. National infrastructure terms take a year, and for most firms the better use of the budget is depth on credentials rather than breadth on head terms.

We freeze your trailing-90-day count of qualified enquiries from organic search on day one. For a construction firm that usually means RFP invitations, pre-qualification requests and site-visit bookings rather than form fills — we agree the definition in writing before anything ships, and [setting the baseline properly](/journal/how-to-set-an-seo-baseline) is the first thing we do. Miss it in 90 days and we keep working free until we beat it. We never promise a specific ranking position for a specific keyword, because nobody controls Google's index. Three clients a month.

faqs.q: Does SEO actually generate construction leads, or is it just a brochure?
faqs.a: Both, and the split depends on your work. Residential and small commercial contracting genuinely generates enquiries from cost and 'near me' searches. Institutional and infrastructure work rarely does — there, the site's job is to survive due diligence after your name is already shortlisted. Measure each accordingly.

faqs.q: What should a construction company's project page include?
faqs.a: Scale in the right unit — sq ft, km, tonnage — contract value as a band, duration from mobilisation to handover, client and consultants with permission, exact scope, and site photographs with captions. Without those numbers it's a gallery, and it convinces neither a procurement reader nor a search engine.

faqs.q: Should residential and infrastructure work sit on the same website?
faqs.a: Only in clearly separated sections with their own navigation, landing pages and enquiry routes. The two buyers search differently and need different proof. If one arm is a small share of revenue, it's often better to stop competing for it online than to dilute the site trying.

faqs.q: Is my company profile PDF enough?
faqs.a: No. PDFs index poorly, load slowly, can't be linked at section level, and can't be updated without republishing the whole file. Everything in the deck — capability, plant list, project data, certifications — should exist as HTML pages. Keep the PDF as a download for people who ask for one.

faqs.q: How do I rank for construction cost per square foot queries?
faqs.a: With a city-specific page built around package tiers, each carrying the actual specification behind it, a clear exclusion list, an as-of date, and links to two completed homes built at that tier. Aggregators can publish the number; only you can publish the houses behind it.

faqs.q: How long before construction SEO shows results?
faqs.a: Branded and credential queries improve within weeks because you're competing with your own absence. Residential cost and local contractor queries usually move in three to six months. National infrastructure terms take a year or more, and are often the wrong place to spend the budget.
